questions.question: Which statement describes the safest assumption when an alarm sounds?

options.text: It is real until it is officially confirmed otherwise.
It is a drill unless smoke is visible.
It is a fault if the alarm is short.
It is real only if other people are leaving.

questions.why: The cause cannot be known from the sound, so the guide says to treat every alarm as real until it is officially confirmed otherwise.
questions.hint: Think about what you can know from the sound alone.

questions.question: You can tell a test from a real alarm by the sound alone.
questions.why: Tests, faults and real fires can sound identical, so the sound is not evidence.
questions.hint: Consider how a test is designed to sound.

questions.question: Which of these is an official confirmation that an alarm is not real?

options.text: A statement from building management, a warden or the emergency services.
Most people staying in their seats.

questions.why: Only people responsible for the building or the response can officially confirm it. Messages, silence and the behaviour of others are not confirmation.
questions.hint: Who is responsible for the building and the response?

questions.question: The way you act in a drill is the way you are likely to act in a real alarm.
questions.why: People repeat the habits they practise, so drills should be taken as seriously as a real alarm.
questions.hint: What do people fall back on under stress?

questions.question: What should you do first when you hear an alarm?

options.text: Stop non-essential tasks and start to leave.
Phone the building manager to ask the cause.
Look for signs of a fire.

questions.why: The first seconds matter. Stopping what you are doing and starting to leave saves time for the exit.
questions.hint: What takes up the first seconds if you do not stop?

questions.question: What may you take with you when leaving?

options.text: Anything you can gather within a minute.
Nothing at all, not even a phone.
Only what you can carry in a few seconds.

questions.why: The guide allows only what can be carried in a few seconds, such as a phone already in hand.
questions.hint: The limit is about time, not about a list of items.

questions.question: It is acceptable to delay your exit briefly to collect belongings that are close by.
questions.why: The guide says never to delay your exit to collect belongings, even when they are close.
questions.hint: Does the distance to the item change the rule?

questions.question: Why should you not go back for a coat that is only a few metres away?

options.text: A detour delays you, blocks others and may take you towards danger.
Coats are not allowed in stairwells.

questions.why: A short detour costs time, can block the route for others and may take you towards the danger.
questions.hint: Think about the others on the route as well as yourself.

questions.question: Which items are best left behind?

options.text: Medicine you need and can reach at once.

questions.why: Bulky or heavy items slow you down, while small items already in your hand cost no time.
questions.hint: Which items take time to pick up or slow you down?

questions.question: Why is an ordinary elevator not used during a fire alarm?

options.text: It may stop between floors, open onto the fire or lose power.
It is slower than the stairs.

questions.why: A lift can trap you between floors, open at a floor affected by the fire or stop when power fails.
questions.hint: Imagine being inside a stopped car.

questions.question: Ordinary elevators should not be used during a fire alarm.
questions.why: The guide says not to use elevators during a fire and to use the stairs.
questions.hint: What does the guide say about stairs and elevators?

questions.question: Which lifts may be used for evacuation?

options.text: Any lift if the stairs are crowded.
The lift nearest to the exit.
Only lifts designated for evacuation and operated by the emergency services or trained staff.

questions.why: Some buildings have designated evacuation lifts, but they are used only under the control of trained staff or the emergency services.
questions.hint: Who operates a lift that is designated for evacuation?

questions.question: How should you move on the stairs?

options.text: At a steady walking pace, holding the handrail.
Side by side, so you can talk.

questions.why: A steady pace and a hand on the rail prevent falls, which would block everyone behind you.
questions.hint: What would a fall do to the people behind you?

questions.question: When should you help another person during an evacuation?

options.text: Only if you are a manager.
Only if it is safe for you.

questions.why: A rescuer who becomes a casualty creates a second problem. Help only if it is safe, otherwise report the person's location.
questions.hint: Consider what happens if the helper is hurt as well.

questions.question: A colleague cannot use the stairs and you are not trained to move them. What do you do?

options.text: Carry them down with a colleague.
Tell them you will report their location, then report it to a warden or responder at once.
Block the stairs until help arrives.

questions.why: Untrained carrying can injure both people and block the route. Reporting the exact location lets responders reach them.
questions.hint: What action helps trained responders most?

questions.question: Which details help responders find someone who could not leave?

options.text: The floor, the room, the nearest landing and how many people are with them.

questions.why: A precise location and the number of people let responders go to the right place with the right help.
questions.hint: How would you describe where someone is to a stranger?

questions.question: If someone is missing, you should go back into the building to look for them.
questions.why: Do not re-enter. Report the missing person's name and last known location to responders.
questions.hint: Who is equipped to search a building during an alarm?

questions.question: Nobody in the room reacts to the alarm. What is the best action?

options.text: Start moving and say clearly: 'Alarm, leave now.'

questions.why: Groups often wait for someone else to act. Starting to move and calling it out breaks the pause.
questions.hint: What happens when everyone waits for someone else?

questions.question: Why do people often delay reacting to an alarm?

options.text: They are not allowed to leave.
They assume it is a drill or a fault and wait for others.

questions.why: Frequent tests and faults teach people to expect a false alarm, and they watch others instead of acting.
questions.hint: What have repeated false alarms taught them?

questions.question: The alarm stops while you are outside. What should you do?

options.text: Go back inside to collect your things.
Stay out until it is officially confirmed that it is safe.
Go back if no one is around.

questions.why: Silence is not confirmation. Stay out until building management, a warden or the emergency services say it is safe.
questions.hint: Does the end of the sound mean the end of the danger?

questions.question: What part of your hand do you use to check whether a closed door is hot?
questions.why: The guide says to feel a closed door with the back of your hand before opening it.

questions.question: A door on your route feels hot. What does the guide tell you to do?

options.text: Do not open it and use another route
Open it fully to let the heat out

questions.why: A hot door suggests fire behind it. Do not open it; use another route.

questions.question: What does the guide say to do first when you reach a closed door?

options.text: Open it quickly and keep moving
Feel it with the back of your hand

questions.why: Check the door first, open a cool door slowly so you can shut it again, and close doors behind you to slow fire and smoke.

questions.question: Why does the guide tell you to stay low in smoke?

options.text: Smoke and hot gases rise, so the air is cleaner near the floor
It is easier to find the exit signs

questions.why: Smoke and hot gases rise, so the cleaner air is near the floor.

questions.question: Breaking a window helps clear smoke from a corridor.
questions.why: Extra air can make a fire grow, and it will not clear your route. The guide says not to break windows to clear smoke.

questions.question: Your route is blocked by smoke. What does the guide list?

options.text: Go to a room with a window, close the door and seal gaps if you can
Wait in the corridor for the smoke to clear
Open every door to let the smoke out

questions.why: If your route is blocked, go to a room with a window, close the door, seal gaps, signal and call. Running through smoke exposes you to the worst air.

questions.question: While moving through smoke, what does the guide suggest you keep on the wall?
questions.why: Keeping one hand on the wall helps you hold your direction when you cannot see well.

questions.question: Where should the assembly point be?

options.text: Away from the building and its entrances
In the car park next to the doors

questions.why: Away from the building and its entrances, so responders have access.

questions.question: Once you are out, you may go back in to fetch a colleague if the smoke looks light.
questions.why: The guide says not to re-enter the building until responders declare it safe.

questions.question: At the assembly point, what do you report about someone who is missing?

options.text: Their name and last known location

questions.why: Report anyone missing and their last known location to the person responsible for the headcount.

questions.question: Several people stand around you. What is the guide's way to make sure the emergency call happens?

options.text: Wait to see whether anyone has called
Point at one person and tell them to call and report back

questions.why: A general request makes people assume someone else has called. Assign one specific person.

questions.question: What should the caller give on an emergency call?

options.text: The location, what happened, the number of injured people and any hazards

questions.why: Give the location, what happened, the number of injured people and any hazards.

questions.question: The caller should hang up as soon as they have given the address.
questions.why: Stay on the line until you are told to hang up.

questions.question: What is the first of the guide's checks of an injured person?

options.text: Check that the scene is safe
Move the person to a better place

questions.why: First make sure the scene is safe so you do not become a second casualty, then check responsiveness, then breathing.

questions.question: For how long do you look, listen and feel for breathing?
questions.why: The guide says to check breathing for up to 10 seconds.

questions.question: Which problem is life-threatening and comes first?
questions.why: Deal with life-threatening problems first: not breathing and severe bleeding.

questions.question: What is the first step to control severe bleeding?

options.text: Press firmly and directly on the wound with a clean cloth
Wash the wound under running water

questions.why: Firm, direct pressure with a clean cloth or dressing is the first step.

questions.question: If the cloth soaks through, you should lift it off and replace it with a fresh one.
questions.why: Lifting the cloth releases pressure and can restart bleeding. Add more layers on top instead.

questions.question: The cloth on a bleeding wound has soaked through. What do you do?

options.text: Remove it and press with a new cloth
Add more layers on top and keep the pressure on
Lift the cloth to check the wound
Stop pressing and wait for help

questions.why: Do not remove the soaked cloth; add more layers on top and keep the pressure on.

questions.question: What is the first step of bleeding care in the guide?

options.text: Keep the person lying down and warm
Press firmly on the wound with a clean cloth

questions.why: Pressure first, add layers rather than lifting, then keep the person lying down and warm and monitor them until help arrives.

questions.question: How long should a burn be cooled under cool running water?
questions.why: Cool the burn under cool running water for 10 to 20 minutes.

questions.question: Which of these is the right treatment for a burn?
questions.why: Do not use ice, butter, oils or toothpaste. Cool running water is the right treatment.

questions.question: A burn on the hand is a reason to seek medical help.
questions.why: The guide lists burns on the face, hands or genitals, large or deep burns, or any doubt, as reasons to seek medical help.

questions.question: A person does not respond but is breathing normally. What does the guide say?

options.text: Sit them up and give them water
Place them in the recovery position and monitor breathing

questions.why: If the person is breathing normally, place them in the recovery position, keep the airway open and monitor breathing.

questions.question: What device can you use, if one is available, when a person is not breathing normally?
questions.why: Use an AED if one is available and follow its prompts.

questions.question: About how fast are chest compressions given?
questions.why: The guide says hard and fast, about 100 to 120 per minute, in the centre of the chest.

questions.question: Which part of a handover to responders comes first?
questions.why: A short, ordered handover: what happened, what you found, what you did and when, and any changes since.

questions.question: A good handover includes the name of any missing person and where they were last seen.
questions.why: The guide says to name any missing person and the last place they were seen.

questions.question: Which detail belongs in a handover?

options.text: Your opinion of how the alarm system was installed
Your view of who caused the incident
The names of everyone in the building

questions.why: A handover covers what happened, what you found, what you did and when, and any changes since.
